title: The Holy Land
full_review:
Writer-director Eitan Gorlin's debut feature, "The Holy Land" (Cavu), examines the temptations of a young rabbinical student who leaves his safe Orthodox world to explore the secular world of Jerusalem.

Essentially a story about the prodigal son, "The Holy Land" subtly underscores the complex cultural and religious conflicts brewing in the sacred city. Yet, what should be the film's strength -- the struggle between a young man's religious convictions and his desires to experience the enticing underworld of Jerusalem -- fails to engage. The uneven coming-of-age tale flits its attention to and fro, and the plodding pace makes the film sag when it should resonate.

When his rabbinical teacher catches Mendy (Oren Rehany) straying from his Torah reading to indulge in some dirty magazines, he off-handedly suggests Mendy get his temptation out of his system with a one-time visit to a prostitute. But after his brief encounter with Sasha (Tchelet Semel), a 19-year-old Russian prostitute he meets at a topless bar, Mendy is smitten.
Convincing his parents that a sabbatical to Jerusalem will reawaken his flagging faith, Mendy finds himself working for Mike (Saul Stein), a loud-mouthed American war photographer who no longer takes pictures but instead owns a dive bar, and, most importantly, is a friend of Sasha's.

Drawing an unflattering picture of Jerusalem as a hotbed for seedy characters and underhanded deeds, director Gorlin's apparently semi-autobiographical account backfires as the film focuses too much on the harsh realities of the city and not enough on Mendy's emotional turmoil. Scenes of an explicit sexual nature are off-putting and detract from the coming-of-age aspect of the film. Several of the plot's strands are at best loosely woven together. For example, Mike's reasons for befriending Mendy are certainly not pure, but hints of terrorist activity are foggy. And the shock ending doesn't quite jell with what's gone on before.

Because of a few explicit sexual encounters, full frontal nudity, some drug use, and intermittent rough language with minimal profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
